title: The Poem in the Armor
tagline: He was the samurai who wrote verses on the night before battle.

scenes.text: Japan, 1183. The Genpei War pits the Taira clan against the Minamoto. Taira no Tadanori — samurai, provincial governor, and devoted poet — rides to the capital as it falls.
The night before the Taira flee Kyoto, Tadanori rides alone to the house of the great poetry master Fujiwara no Shunzei. He leaves a scroll of his poems — asking that even one be remembered.

params.title: Out of the Burning Capital
params.intro: Kyoto, summer 1183: the Minamoto close in. The child emperor cannot fight — he cannot help take a raider, not even as the far side of a sandwich. Your four guards must do all the fighting while he runs for a corner.
params.fact: When the Taira abandoned Kyoto in the seventh month of 1183, they took the five-year-old Emperor Antoku and the three sacred regalia with them, so that wherever the clan went, the throne went too.

challenge.instruction: While the clan escorts the boy emperor out of Kyoto, Tadanori turns back alone toward Shunzei’s gate. Guard the emperor’s flight and get him clear of the closing ring.
challenge.fact: Tadanori was one of the leading waka poets of his generation, a student of the master Fujiwara no Shunzei. On the eve of the Taira clan's final flight from Kyoto, he rode back alone through the night to deliver a scroll of his poems to Shunzei — asking only that one be included in the imperial anthology. One was: it appears in the Senzai Wakashū without his name, since he died a rebel.

scenes.text: The Taira retreat south. For two years they fight a losing war — islands, sea battles, the slow narrowing of a doomed world. Tadanori composes poems throughout.

challenge.instruction: The Taira take to their ships and the Minamoto hold every harbour mouth. Shift the crowding boats aside and steer the imperial vessel out to open water.
challenge.fact: Because Tadanori died on the losing side of the Genpei War, his poem was included in the Senzai Wakashū as 'anonymous' — it would have been politically unacceptable to honor a Taira rebel by name. Yet the poem's inclusion was itself an act of aesthetic respect. Everyone knew whose poem it was, and that silent knowledge became part of the poem's beauty.

scenes.text: Battle of Ichi-no-Tani, 1184: the Minamoto attack from the cliffs above. In the chaos, Tadanori is unhorsed and falls into single combat. He is killed — a poem on his person reveals his name.

params.title: Fukuhara Abandoned, 1183
params.rule: Burn the stores, spare the quay
params.intro: The Minamoto are coming. Torch houses so the wind carries the fire through every storehouse (🌾) before they arrive, and pull down houses so it never reaches the stone quay (🏰). You have fewer torches than storehouses.

challenge.instruction: In 1183 the Taira abandon the capital, then Fukuhara, the port Kiyomori built for the ships of Song China. Leave nothing for the Minamoto: let the wind carry fire through the storehouses, and keep it off the stone quay where the fleet waits.
challenge.fact: The tale of Tadanori riding back to his poetry master on the night of defeat became one of the most celebrated stories in Japanese literary history. It appears in the Heike Monogatari — the great narrative of the Genpei War — as the moment when a warrior reveals that poetry, not victory, is what he cannot bear to leave behind.

scenes.text: His killer weeps. Even an enemy honors a warrior who wrote such verse. The poem found in his armor that day: 'As the evening dark descends, I rest beneath this cherry tree — a flower is my inn.'

challenge.instruction: Tadanori’s killer unties a paper from the fallen warrior’s quiver. Read the poem shape by shape and learn whose life he has taken.
challenge.fact: The Heike Monogatari opens with the most famous line in Japanese literature: 'The sound of the Gion Shoja bells echoes the impermanence of all things.' It was not read but performed — chanted to biwa accompaniment by traveling monks who served as medieval Japan's living archive of history and loss.

scenes.text: Fujiwara no Shunzei includes one of Tadanori's poems in the imperial anthology — anonymously, because Tadanori died as an enemy of the crown. The poem outlives the war and the clan.

challenge.instruction: Years later Shunzei unrolls the scroll Tadanori left at his gate. Find the roller that lines up the words and read how the anthology will name him.
challenge.fact: The Battle of Ichi-no-Tani (1184) was a Minamoto tactical masterpiece: while one force engaged the Taira from the front, Minamoto Yoshitsune led cavalry down a cliff believed to be impassable. The surprise attack from above broke the Taira position. Tadanori died fighting in this rout — killed by a Minamoto warrior who recognized him only by a poem tucked inside his armour.

params.title: Dan-no-ura, 1185
params.intro: In the strait the Taira ships keep moving: each turn every ship moves one square along its row, turning about at the shore. You cannot see them — until one is hit and burns.

challenge.instruction: Spring 1185: the last Taira fleet meets the Minamoto in the strait of Dan-no-ura, where the tide runs hard and turns at midday. The ships never stop moving with the current. Find them before the day is spent.
challenge.fact: At Dan-no-ura, in the Kanmon Strait, the Taira fleet was destroyed on 25 April 1185. As the battle turned, Kiyomori's widow leapt into the sea with the child emperor Antoku in her arms, and the clan Tadanori died for was gone.

scenes.speaker: Taira no Tadanori
scenes.text: Ibn Battuta waits at Changan, but nothing is happening there, and without an event there is no fight. I will go first; the turn after I arrive, play the Art Critique card on Changan and we attack.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 3 · Starting an Event. Deploy Taira no Tadanori to Changan and End Turn. Next turn play the Art Critique card there, add your follower and win one attack.
challenge.fact: Event cards start a scenario at a location where you already have a Great Person, and only one who arrived on an earlier turn can start it. A local event keeps running until a player ends it.
